title: The rook in a busy position
outcomes: Decides what kind of piece stands on a named square before drawing its lines
Taps every square the rook can reach when other pieces fill the board, one line at a time
Tells an own blocker from an enemy blocker and a piece on the line from one beside it
Says whether a rook can reach a far square in one move, and spots the one piece that stops it
Finds a second route round a single blocker and says it takes two moves

steps.text: In a real game nobody tells you which piece to think about, and the board is full. You already know how a rook slides. This lesson is about reading a crowded board without mistakes. First watch one worked example, then try a quiet board yourself.

steps.caption: A busier board. The white rook is on d4. Walk outward from it, one direction at a time, and stop at the first piece you meet.

claims.statement: The piece on d4 is a white rook.

steps.caption: Up. d5 is empty, then White's own pawn stands on d6.

line.say: The rook may stop on d5. Its own pawn on d6 is the first piece, so d6 and beyond are closed.

claims.statement: The rook can go to d5.
The rook cannot land on its own pawn.
The rook cannot jump the pawn.

steps.caption: Down. Nothing stands on d3, d2 or d1.

line.say: Three empty squares and then the edge: the rook can stop on any of them, even the last.

claims.statement: The rook can go to d3.
The rook can go to d1.

steps.caption: Left. c4 is empty, then a black knight stands on b4.

line.say: The first piece is an enemy knight, so the rook may take it. The slide ends there, and a4 is out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can go to c4.
The rook can take on b4.
The rook cannot go past the knight to a4.
A black knight stands on b4.

steps.caption: Right. e4 and f4 are empty, then White's own pawn stands on g4.

line.say: Two free squares. The rook stops on f4, one short of its own pawn. h4 behind the pawn is closed.

claims.statement: The rook can go to f4.
The rook cannot land on its own pawn.
The rook cannot jump the pawn.

steps.caption: All together: eight squares. One up, three down, two left (one of them a capture), two right. The bishop on e5 and the pawns on g7 and h7 are on none of the rook's lines, so they change nothing.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d4 can move to.

steps.caption: For comparison, the same rook on an empty board reaches fourteen squares. Every blocker on a line removes squares, so a busy board gives a smaller number.

claims.statement: On an empty board the rook on d4 reaches exactly these fourteen squares.

steps.text: **Three questions, in this order.** What piece is it? Which lines does it travel on? What is the first piece on each line: nothing, one of yours, or an enemy? A piece standing on a line is a **blocker**. [I] Walking outward line by line probably works better than scanning the whole board, because each line ends at its first piece.
Nobody will tell you the piece is a rook. A different piece takes a different walk, so name the piece before you draw a single line. Here is the same board again, with other pieces on d4.

steps.caption: A bishop on d4. It travels on diagonals, so the squares it reaches are not the rook's squares at all. Its own bishop on e5 closes one diagonal at once.

line.say: Up and to the left along the diagonal to the edge: three squares, a move no rook can make.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the bishop on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white bishop.

steps.caption: A knight on d4. It jumps in an L, and jumping ignores blockers. Eight squares, and not one is on the rook's lines.

line.say: The knight leaps two squares up and one across. What stands in between does not matter.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the knight on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white knight.

steps.caption: A queen on d4 does both jobs: all the rook's squares and all the bishop's squares, fifteen in total here. Name the piece and you know which lines to walk.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on d4 can move to.
The piece on d4 is a white queen.

steps.text: The first piece on a line ends it. If it is yours, the rook stops one square short. If it is an enemy, the rook may take it and then stops there. It never goes through, and a piece beside the line, not on it, blocks nothing.

steps.caption: The white knight on a4 is the first piece on the a-file.

line.say: The rook can come up to a3. The knight is its own piece, so a4 is off limits and a5 to a8 are out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can go to a3.
The rook cannot land on its own knight.
The rook cannot reach a8.
A white knight stands on a4.

steps.caption: Now the first piece on the file is an enemy knight, with a black pawn behind it on a6.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. Taking ends the slide, so the pawn on a6 is not reachable this move.

claims.statement: The rook can take on a4.
The rook cannot go past the knight.
The rook cannot reach the pawn behind the knight.
A black knight stands on a4.

steps.caption: The first piece can be right next to the rook. The black pawn on d5 is an enemy, so the rook may take it at once.

line.say: The nearest square is a capture. The slide ends there, so d6 and beyond stay out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can take on d5.
The rook cannot go past the pawn.
A black pawn stands on d5.

steps.caption: The black knight sits on d4, on neither of the rook's lines. The a-file is clear, so the rook goes all the way up. Only a piece on the line counts.

line.say: Seven squares up the file in one move. The knight is beside the rook's route, so it does not matter.

claims.statement: The rook can go from a1 to a8.
A black knight stands on d4.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: A white knight now stands on e3. Predict first: can the rook still reach g3?

steps.caption: A far target behind an enemy piece. The black pawn on c3 is the first piece on the c-file.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn and the slide ends. It cannot carry on to c8.

claims.statement: The rook can take on c3.
The rook cannot reach c8.
A black pawn stands on c3.

steps.text: **Counting moves without a board.** Is the target on my rank or file? Is any piece on the line between? If nothing, one move. If one blocker is all that stops it, look for another line that reaches the same square: that is often two moves. [H] Beginners may miss a blocker mostly because they scan the line too fast; naming each square aloud may help.

steps.caption: The white knight on a4 blocks the a-file, so the top row is not reachable in one move. The rook sidesteps to a clear file. [I] A second blocker, or blockers on the neighbouring files, can make it three moves or more.

line.say: Step sideways onto the b-file. The rook does not need a2 or a3.
Black moves the king. Nothing changes on the b-file.
The b-file is clear all the way. Here one blocker cost one extra move.

claims.statement: The rook cannot reach a8 in one move.
After the sidestep, the rook on b1 attacks the whole b-file up to b8.

steps.caption: A common slip: trying to take your own pawn. The pawn on d5 is white, like the rook. The square is off limits.

line.say: Down is free. Up, the first piece is a friend, so the rook goes nowhere on that side.

claims.statement: The rook cannot take its own pawn.
The rook can go down to d3.

steps.caption: Another slip: turning a corner. A rook goes in one direction per move, so f6 takes two moves, never one.

line.say: First slide right along the rank.
Black's king moves.
Then slide up the f-file. Two moves, two straight lines.

claims.statement: The rook cannot reach f6 in one move.
The rook can slide to f4 first.

steps.caption: Pieces on your own side block too. The rook on a1 can only come up to a3, because the other white rook on a4 is its first piece.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on a1 can move to.

steps.caption: Friends can shut a rook in on one line and leave it free on the other. Here the knight and the bishop close the first rank, so only the d-file is open.

line.say: Six squares up the open file in one move. The rank gave it nothing, but the file is clear.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d1 can move to.

steps.text: **A blocker has a colour, and the colour matters later.** An own piece on the line ends the slide, and the rook stands guard over it. An enemy piece on the line ends the slide too, and the rook attacks it. Same stop, opposite meaning. Watch both on a board.

steps.caption: The knight on d3 is White's own. The rook cannot take it, but the rook protects it: if an enemy piece took the knight, the rook could take back. The black pawn on d5 is behind the knight and out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 covers d2 and the own knight on d3, and nothing beyond.
The rook cannot capture its own knight.

steps.caption: Now the knight on d4 is Black's. The rook attacks it and may take it. Same line, same stop, but the blocker is a target instead of a friend.

line.say: The rook takes the knight and the slide ends on d4.

claims.statement: The rook on d1 attacks the knight on d4 and nothing beyond it.
The rook can take the knight on d4.

steps.caption: A trap for the line-walker. The white rook on c1 stands between its king and the black rook on a1. If it left the first rank, its king would be in check, so up the c-file is closed to it. It may only slide along the rank. It still sees the c-file; it is not allowed to use it.

claims.statement: These are exactly the legal squares of the pinned rook on c1.
The rook on c1 still attacks the whole c-file, pins ignored.
The pinned rook cannot move up the c-file.

steps.text: **Attacked is not the same as allowed.** A rook attacks every square up to its first blocker. It may only go to those squares if the move leaves its own king safe. [I] Counting a rook's squares first by lines, then asking whether its king is in the way, probably avoids most slips here.
Sometimes the right answer is *none*, and sometimes the rook's lines are the wrong lines altogether. Look at a rook boxed in by its own side. One piece moving changes everything.

steps.caption: The rook in the corner has a pawn above it and a knight beside it: no legal move at all.

line.say: The knight moves away, which opens the first rank.
Black moves the king.
Now the rook has room: one piece out of the way gave it a line.

claims.statement: The rook on a1 has no legal move.
The piece on a1 is a white rook.

steps.caption: A hint of why we care. On a file with no pawns, the rook crosses the board in one move. [I] An open file lets a rook cross the board in one move, which is probably why open lines matter so much to rooks. A later lesson looks at this.

line.say: Six squares in one move, from the first rank to the seventh, because nothing stands on the file.

claims.statement: The rook can go from e1 to e7.

steps.caption: On an empty board a rook reaches fourteen squares from any square, corner or centre. Mobility depends on what stands on its lines, not on where the rook stands.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on a1 can move to.

steps.text: Now the unlabelled round. Nothing tells you which piece to think about, and one position will not be a rook at all. For each one: name the piece, walk its lines, stop at the first piece. A wrong answer shows which step you skipped.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend how to count the rook's squares from d4 in the first position of this lesson, and what changes if a blocker is an enemy rather than your own. Write it in your own words before you read on.

fields.label: A position from this lesson where a piece blocks a rook, and whose piece it is:

steps.text: **Compare.** *Name the piece first, then walk each of its lines outward. A rook stops at the first piece on a line: it stops one short of its own, and may take an enemy piece and stop there. A piece beside the line blocks nothing, and one blocker may cost one extra move.*

steps.prompt: Think of an answer you hesitated on. Which piece was in the way, and was it yours or the enemy's? What will you look at first next time? (optional)
